sections.title: Section A — common to Mathematics and Applied Mathematics (compulsory)

questions.sub_topic: At least two heads with three coins
questions.question: Three fair coins are tossed. The probability of getting at least two heads is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
Given: 8 equally likely outcomes
Formula: \(P(X \ge 2) = P(X = 2) + P(X = 3)\)
Step 1: Exactly two heads: \(HHT, HTH, THH\), 3 outcomes; three heads: \(HHH\), 1 outcome
Step 2: \(P = \dfrac{3 + 1}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) (A) is exactly two heads. \(\dfrac{7}{8}\) (D) is at least one head.
Key point: "At least two" includes two and three.

questions.sub_topic: Facts about optimal solutions of an LPP
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a linear programming problem:
(A) If the feasible region is bounded and non-empty, the objective function has both a maximum and a minimum.
(B) If an optimal value exists, it occurs at a corner point of the feasible region.
(C) On an unbounded feasible region, a maximum may not exist.
(D) The feasible region of a linear programming problem is always bounded.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: constraints such as \(x + y \ge 4\), \(x, y \ge 0\) give an unbounded region.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are the corner-point theorems of linear programming. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: A bounded region guarantees both optimal values; an unbounded one needs a further check.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Solving two equations by the matrix method
questions.question: Using the matrix method, the solution of \(x + 2y = 4\) and \(3x - y = 5\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(x = 2, y = 1\)
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&-1\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}4\\5\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: \(X = A^{-1}B\), \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}\,A\)
Step 1: \(|A| = -1 - 6 = -7\); \(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix}-1&-2\\-3&1\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(\text{adj}\,A \cdot B = \begin{bmatrix}-4 - 10\\-12 + 5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-14\\-7\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 3: \(X = \dfrac{1}{-7}\begin{bmatrix}-14\\-7\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\)
Common mistake: (B) forgets that \(|A|\) is negative. (A) swaps \(x\) and \(y\).
Key point: Check by substituting: \(2 + 2 = 4\) ✓, \(6 - 1 = 5\) ✓.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\), then \(AB\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\3&0\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: rows of \(A\), columns of \(B\)
Formula: \((AB)_{ij} = \) row \(i\) of \(A\) · column \(j\) of \(B\)
Step 1: Row 1: \((1)(2) + (2)(1) = 4\); \((1)(1) + (2)(0) = 1\)
Step 2: Row 2: \((0)(2) + (3)(1) = 3\); \((0)(1) + (3)(0) = 0\)
Common mistake: (B) is \(BA\); matrix multiplication is not commutative. (C) multiplies entry by entry.
Key point: Row of the first matrix times column of the second.

questions.sub_topic: Four measures of one probability distribution
questions.question:
A random variable \(X\) takes the values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities \(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{6}\). Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(P(X \ge 1)\)
(B) \(E(X)\)
(C) \(E(X^2)\)
(D) \(\text{Var}(X)\)

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{5}{3}\)
(II) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
(III) \(\dfrac{5}{9}\)
(IV) \(\dfrac{10}{3}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Given: values 1, 2, 3; probabilities \(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{6}\)
Step 1: \(P(X \ge 2) = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) (II)
Step 2: \(E(X) = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) (I)
Step 3: \(E(X^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{10}{3}\) (IV)
Step 4: \(\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{10}{3} - \dfrac{25}{9} = \dfrac{5}{9}\) (III)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the first two. (C) swaps \(E(X^2)\) and the variance. (D) swaps \(E(X)\) and \(E(X^2)\).
Key point: \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\).

questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x}\) (\(x, y > 0\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(y = Cx\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x}\)
Formula: separate: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = \dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Step 1: \(\log y = \log x + \log C\)
Step 2: \(y = Cx\)
Common mistake: (C) gets the sign wrong (that solves \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{y}{x}\)). (D) solves \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\).
Key point: Writing the constant as \(\log C\) combines the logarithms neatly.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Area of a circle changing with its radius
questions.question: The rate of change of the area of a circle with respect to its radius \(r\), when \(r = 5\) cm, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(10\pi\) cm²/cm
Given: \(A = \pi r^2\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 2\pi r\)
Step 1: At \(r = 5\): \(2\pi(5) = 10\pi\)
Common mistake: \(25\pi\) (B) is the area itself, not its rate of change.
Key point: Rate of change means the derivative.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\log(1 + x^2) + C\)
Given: the numerator \(2x\) is the derivative of \(1 + x^2\)
Formula: \(\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx = \log|f(x)| + C\)
Step 1: Put \(t = 1 + x^2\), \(dt = 2x\,dx\): \(\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log t\)
Step 2: \(= \log(1 + x^2) + C\) (no modulus needed, since \(1 + x^2 > 0\))
Common mistake: (A) and (C) use the \(\tan^{-1}\) formula, which fits \(\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}\), not \(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\).
Key point: Check whether the numerator is the derivative of the denominator.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.question: The function \(f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2\) is strictly decreasing on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \((-\infty, -1) \cup (0, 1)\)
Given: \(f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2\)
Formula: strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\)
Step 1: \(f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4x = 4x(x - 1)(x + 1)\); critical points \(-1, 0, 1\)
Step 2: Signs of \(f'\): negative on \((-\infty, -1)\), positive on \((-1, 0)\), negative on \((0, 1)\), positive on \((1, \infty)\)
Step 3: Decreasing on \((-\infty, -1) \cup (0, 1)\)
Common mistake: (A) is where \(f\) is increasing. (D) misses the interval to the left of \(-1\).
Key point: With three critical points, test the sign on all four intervals.

questions.sub_topic: Order of a linear second-order equation
questions.question: The order of the differential equation \(2x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 3\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2\)
Given: derivatives present: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\)
Formula: order = order of the highest derivative
Step 1: The highest derivative is \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the order is 2
Common mistake: \(3\) (B) reads the coefficient \(-3\) or the power of \(x\) as the order.
Key point: Coefficients do not affect the order.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.question: The maximum value of \(f(x) = xe^{-x}\) for \(x \ge 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{e}\)
Given: \(f(x) = xe^{-x}\)
Formula: \(f'(x) = 0\), then check the sign change
Step 1: \(f'(x) = e^{-x} - xe^{-x} = e^{-x}(1 - x)\)
Step 2: \(f' > 0\) for \(x < 1\) and \(f' < 0\) for \(x > 1\), so \(x = 1\) is a maximum
Step 3: \(f(1) = e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e}\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (A) gives the point \(x = 1\), not the value. \(0\) (D) is the value at the end point \(x = 0\).
Key point: Answer the question asked: the maximum value is \(f(1)\).

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx = 2\)
(B) \(\displaystyle\int e^{2x}\,dx = e^{2x} + C\)
(C) \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}x^3\,dx = 0\)
(D) \(\displaystyle\int_0^{1}2x\,dx = 1\)
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A) \([-\cos x]_0^{\pi} = 1 + 1 = 2\). (C) \(x^3\) is odd, so the integral over \([-1, 1]\) is 0. (D) \([x^2]_0^1 = 1\).
Why not the others: (B) is false: \(\int e^{2x}dx = \dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x} + C\). Option (B) includes it; (A) and (C) leave out true statements.
Key point: The coefficient of \(x\) in an exponent divides the result.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Determinant of a scalar multiple of an inverse
questions.question: If \(A\) is a square matrix of order 2 with \(|A| = 4\), then \(|2A^{-1}|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1\)
Given: \(n = 2\), \(|A| = 4\)
Formula: \(|kB| = k^n|B|\), \(|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\)
Step 1: \(|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{4}\)
Step 2: \(|2A^{-1}| = 2^2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 1\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (A) uses \(k\) instead of \(k^2\). \(16\) (C) uses \(|A|\) instead of \(|A^{-1}|\).
Key point: A scalar comes out of a determinant raised to the order of the matrix.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.question: If \(A\) is a square matrix of order 3 with \(|A| = 2\), then \(|\text{adj}(2A)|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(256\)
Given: \(n = 3\), \(|A| = 2\)
Formula: \(|\text{adj}\,B| = |B|^{n-1}\), \(|kA| = k^n|A|\)
Step 1: \(|2A| = 2^3 \times 2 = 16\)
Step 2: \(|\text{adj}(2A)| = |2A|^2 = 16^2 = 256\)
Common mistake: \(16\) (A) stops at \(|2A|\). \(32\) (C) takes \(\text{adj}(2A) = 2\,\text{adj}\,A\), giving \(2^3 \times 4\); in fact \(\text{adj}(2A) = 2^{2}\,\text{adj}\,A\). \(64\) (B) is \(4^3\), leaving out the factor \(|\text{adj}\,A| = 4\).
Key point: Find \(|2A|\) first, then apply the adjoint rule.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of sin x + cos x
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(2\)
Given: limits \(0\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Formula: \(\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x\), \(\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x\)
Step 1: \([-\cos x + \sin x]_0^{\pi/2} = (0 + 1) - (-1 + 0)\)
Step 2: \(= 1 + 1 = 2\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (B) takes \(\int \sin x\,dx = \cos x\), so the two parts cancel.
Key point: The integral of \(\sin x\) carries a minus sign.

questions.sub_topic: Integrating factor when P = tan x
questions.question: The integrating factor of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y\tan x = \sec x\) (\(0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\sec x\)
Given: \(P = \tan x\)
Formula: I.F. \(= e^{\int P\,dx}\)
Step 1: \(\int \tan x\,dx = \log\sec x\)
Step 2: I.F. \(= e^{\log\sec x} = \sec x\)
Common mistake: (C) puts \(P\) itself in the exponent without integrating. (A) takes \(\int \tan x\,dx = \log\cos x\), dropping the minus sign.
Key point: \(\int \tan x\,dx = -\log\cos x = \log\sec x\).

questions.sub_topic: Two children, at least one a boy
questions.question: A family has two children. Given that at least one of them is a boy, the probability that both are boys is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
Given: sample space \(\{BB, BG, GB, GG\}\), equally likely
Formula: \(P(E \mid F) = \dfrac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)}\)
Step 1: \(F\) = at least one boy \(= \{BB, BG, GB\}\), \(P(F) = \dfrac{3}{4}\)
Step 2: \(E \cap F = \{BB\}\), probability \(\dfrac{1}{4}\)
Step 3: \(P(E \mid F) = \dfrac{1/4}{3/4} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (A) treats the other child independently, but the condition does not say which child is a boy. \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) (B) ignores the condition.
Key point: The condition shrinks the sample space to three outcomes.

questions.question:
For \(Z = 3x + 2y\) on the feasible region with corner points \((0, 0)\), \((5, 0)\), \((4, 3)\) and \((0, 6)\), consider the following statements:
(A) The maximum value of \(Z\) is 18.
(B) The maximum occurs at \((4, 3)\).
(C) The minimum value of \(Z\) is 0.
(D) \(Z\) has the same value at \((5, 0)\) and \((0, 6)\).
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: \(Z\) at the corners is \(0, 15, 18, 12\). Only (D) is false: \(Z(5, 0) = 15\) but \(Z(0, 6) = 12\).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) agree with the table. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Tabulate \(Z\) at every corner before judging any claim.

questions.question: The distance between the parallel lines \(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\) and \(\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\sqrt{6}\)
Given: \(\vec{b} = (1, -1, 1)\), \(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = (1, -1, -2)\)
Formula: \(d = \dfrac{|\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&-1&1\\1&-1&-2\end{vmatrix} = (2 + 1)\hat{i} - (-2 - 1)\hat{j} + (-1 + 1)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\)
Step 2: Its magnitude is \(3\sqrt{2}\); \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{3}\)
Step 3: \(d = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{6}\)
Common mistake: \(3\sqrt{2}\) (B) forgets to divide by \(|\vec{b}|\).
Key point: For parallel lines, use the cross product with the common direction.

questions.sub_topic: Dot product from the size of the cross product
questions.question: For vectors with \(|\vec{a}| = 2\), \(|\vec{b}| = 3\) and \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = 3\), the angle between them is acute. Then \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3\sqrt{3}\)
Given: \(|\vec{a}||\vec{b}| = 6\)
Formula: \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta\), \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\); acute, so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
Step 2: \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 6\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = 6 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}\)
Common mistake: \(3\) (A) uses \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\), mixing up sine and cosine. \(6\) (B) assumes the vectors are parallel.
Key point: Cross product goes with sine; dot product goes with cosine.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + C\)
Given: \(\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\)
Formula: \(\int \cos 2x\,dx = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\int \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}dx = \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + C\)
Common mistake: (B) is \(\int \cos^2 x\,dx\). (A) uses the power rule on \(\sin x\) as if it were \(x\).
Key point: Lower the power with a double-angle identity.

questions.sub_topic: Odd and even parts over a symmetric interval
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(x^3 + |x|)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1\)
Given: \(x^3\) is odd; \(|x|\) is even
Formula: \(\int_{-a}^{a}f = 0\) for odd \(f\); \(= 2\int_0^a f\) for even \(f\)
Step 1: \(\int_{-1}^{1}x^3dx = 0\)
Step 2: \(\int_{-1}^{1}|x|dx = 2\int_0^1 x\,dx = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\)
Step 3: Total \(= 1\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (B) treats \(|x|\) as odd as well. \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (D) integrates \(|x|\) over \([0, 1]\) only.
Key point: Split the integrand into odd and even parts.

questions.question: The area of the triangle with vertices \((2, 1)\), \((5, 1)\) and \((3, 5)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(6\) sq units
Given: \((x_1, y_1) = (2, 1)\), \((x_2, y_2) = (5, 1)\), \((x_3, y_3) = (3, 5)\)
Formula: Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{vmatrix}x_1&y_1&1\\x_2&y_2&1\\x_3&y_3&1\end{vmatrix}\right|\)
Step 1: \(\begin{vmatrix}2&1&1\\5&1&1\\3&5&1\end{vmatrix} = 2(1 - 5) - 1(5 - 3) + 1(25 - 3) = -8 - 2 + 22 = 12\)
Step 2: Area \(= \dfrac{12}{2} = 6\)
Common mistake: \(12\) (B) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). \(8\) (C) uses \(+1\) instead of \(-1\) for the second cofactor sign (\(-8 + 2 + 22 = 16\)).
Key point: Check with base × height: base 3, height 4, area 6 ✓.

questions.question: The number of matrices of order \(2 \times 2\) whose every entry is 0 or 1 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(16\)
Given: 4 entries, 2 choices for each
Formula: multiplication principle
Step 1: \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^4 = 16\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (A) counts the entries, not the matrices. \(8\) (C) uses \(2 \times 4\).
Key point: Each entry is chosen independently.

questions.sub_topic: Unknown vertex from a given area
questions.question: The area of the triangle with vertices \((k, 0)\), \((4, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\) is 4 sq units. Then \(k\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(0\) or \(8\)
Given: area \(= 4\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{vmatrix}k&0&1\\4&0&1\\0&2&1\end{vmatrix}\right| = 4\)
Step 1: \(\begin{vmatrix}k&0&1\\4&0&1\\0&2&1\end{vmatrix} = k(0 - 2) - 0 + 1(8 - 0) = 8 - 2k\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{2}|8 - 2k| = 4 \Rightarrow |8 - 2k| = 8\)
Step 3: \(8 - 2k = 8 \Rightarrow k = 0\), or \(8 - 2k = -8 \Rightarrow k = 8\)
Common mistake: (A) and (C) drop the modulus and keep one sign only.
Key point: Area uses the absolute value, so set the determinant equal to \(\pm\) twice the area.

questions.sub_topic: Number of relations on a two-element set
questions.question: The number of relations on a set with 2 elements is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(16\)
Given: \(A \times A\) has \(2 \times 2 = 4\) elements
Formula: a relation is any subset of \(A \times A\); a set with \(m\) elements has \(2^m\) subsets
Step 1: \(2^4 = 16\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (A) counts the ordered pairs, not the subsets.
Key point: Number of relations on an \(n\)-element set \(= 2^{n^2}\).

questions.question: The value of \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)
Given: \(\cos^{-1} \in [0, \pi]\), \(\sin^{-1} \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\)
Formula: \(\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x\)
Step 1: \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
Step 2: \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
Step 3: Sum \(= \dfrac{2\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (B) drops the minus sign and uses \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). \(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (C) uses \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), which is outside \([0, \pi]\).
Key point: \(\cos^{-1}\) of a negative number lies in \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).

questions.sub_topic: Number of onto functions onto a two-element set
questions.question: The number of onto functions from \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) to \(\{a, b\}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(6\)
Given: each of 3 elements can go to \(a\) or \(b\)
Formula: onto = all functions − functions missing an image
Step 1: All functions: \(2^3 = 8\)
Step 2: Not onto: all to \(a\), or all to \(b\): 2 functions
Step 3: Onto functions: \(8 - 2 = 6\)
Common mistake: \(8\) (A) counts all functions. \(2\) (B) counts the two constant functions that must be removed.
Key point: Onto means every element of the codomain is used.

questions.question: If \(P(A) = 0.4\) and \(P(B \mid A) = 0.5\), then \(P(A \cap B)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(0.2\)
Given: \(P(A) = 0.4\), \(P(B \mid A) = 0.5\)
Formula: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)\)
Step 1: \(0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2\)
Common mistake: \(0.8\) (C) divides instead of multiplying. \(0.9\) (B) adds.
Key point: "And" with a conditional probability means multiply.

questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} + \tan\dfrac{y}{x}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\sin\dfrac{y}{x} = Cx\)
Given: put \(y = vx\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)
Formula: separate \(v\) and \(x\)
Step 1: \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = v + \tan v \Rightarrow \cot v\,dv = \dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Step 2: \(\log|\sin v| = \log|x| + \log|C|\)
Step 3: \(\sin\dfrac{y}{x} = Cx\)
Common mistake: (B) integrates \(\cot v\) as \(\log\cos v\). (D) writes the constant as \(+C\) after taking antilogs.
Key point: \(\int \cot v\,dv = \log|\sin v|\).

questions.question:
For the line segment joining \(P(1, 2, 3)\) and \(Q(3, 6, 7)\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Direction ratios of \(PQ\)
(B) Direction cosines of \(PQ\)
(C) Length \(PQ\)
(D) Midpoint of \(PQ\)

List-II
(I) \((2, 4, 5)\)
(II) \(6\)
(III) \(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\)
(IV) \(2, 4, 4\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Given: \(Q - P = (2, 4, 4)\)
Step 1: Direction ratios \(2, 4, 4\) (IV)
Step 2: Length \(= \sqrt{4 + 16 + 16} = 6\) (II)
Step 3: Direction cosines \(= \dfrac{2}{6}, \dfrac{4}{6}, \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\) (III)
Step 4: Midpoint \(= \left(\dfrac{1 + 3}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{3 + 7}{2}\right) = (2, 4, 5)\) (I)
Common mistake: (B) swaps the direction ratios and cosines. (C) swaps the cosines and the length. (D) swaps the length and the midpoint.
Key point: Direction cosines are direction ratios divided by the length.

questions.sub_topic: Derivative after an inverse trigonometric substitution
questions.question: For \(-1 < x < 1\), \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2}\right)\right]\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}\)
Given: put \(x = \tan\theta\) with \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta} = \tan 2\theta\)
Step 1: \(\tan^{-1}(\tan 2\theta) = 2\theta = 2\tan^{-1}x\), since \(2\theta\) lies in \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(2\tan^{-1}x) = \dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}\)
Common mistake: (A) forgets the factor 2 from \(2\theta\).
Key point: Simplify with a substitution before differentiating.

questions.question: The function \(f(x) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}, & x \ne 3\\k, & x = 3\end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 3\). Then \(k\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(6\)
Given: \(f(3) = k\)
Formula: continuity needs \(\lim_{x \to 3}f(x) = f(3)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = \dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{x - 3} = x + 3\) for \(x \ne 3\)
Step 2: \(\lim_{x \to 3}(x + 3) = 6\), so \(k = 6\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (B) substitutes \(x = 3\) in the numerator only. \(9\) (C) uses \(x^2\) at 3.
Key point: Cancel the common factor before taking the limit.

questions.sub_topic: Four rates of change at size 3
questions.question:
For a radius or edge of length 3 units, match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Rate of change of the area of a circle with respect to its radius
(B) Rate of change of the volume of a sphere with respect to its radius
(C) Rate of change of the surface area of a cube with respect to its edge
(D) Rate of change of the volume of a cube with respect to its edge

List-II
(I) \(36\pi\)
(II) \(27\)
(III) \(6\pi\)
(IV) \(36\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Given: length 3
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d}{dr}(\pi r^2) = 2\pi r = 6\pi\) (III)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{d}{dr}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) = 4\pi r^2 = 36\pi\) (I)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{d}{da}(6a^2) = 12a = 36\) (IV)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{d}{da}(a^3) = 3a^2 = 27\) (II)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the circle and the sphere. (B) swaps the two cube rates. (D) mixes up \(36\pi\) and \(36\).
Key point: Write the formula first, then differentiate.

questions.sub_topic: Angle for which A + Aᵀ = I
questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}\) and \(A + A^T = I\), then \(\theta\) (with \(0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\)
Given: \(A^T = \begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: equate corresponding entries
Step 1: \(A + A^T = \begin{bmatrix}2\cos\theta&0\\0&2\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(2\cos\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (A) solves \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\) instead.
Key point: The sine terms cancel in \(A + A^T\).

questions.question: Urn I has 3 white and 2 black balls; urn II has 4 white and 4 black balls. A fair coin is tossed: heads, a ball is drawn from urn I; tails, from urn II. The probability that the ball drawn is white is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{11}{20}\)
Given: \(P(E_1) = P(E_2) = \dfrac{1}{2}\); \(P(W \mid E_1) = \dfrac{3}{5}\), \(P(W \mid E_2) = \dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Formula: \(P(W) = P(E_1)P(W \mid E_1) + P(E_2)P(W \mid E_2)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{5} + \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{1}{4}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{6}{20} + \dfrac{5}{20} = \dfrac{11}{20}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{7}{13}\) (A) pools the balls of both urns. \(\dfrac{3}{10}\) (D) keeps only the urn I term.
Key point: Weight each urn's probability by the chance of choosing that urn.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral by substitution: x e^(x²)
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 xe^{x^2}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{e - 1}{2}\)
Given: put \(t = x^2\), \(dt = 2x\,dx\); \(x = 0 \to t = 0\), \(x = 1 \to t = 1\)
Formula: \(\int_0^1 xe^{x^2}dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^1 e^t dt\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{2}[e^t]_0^1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(e - 1)\)
Common mistake: \(e - 1\) (A) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) from \(dt = 2x\,dx\). \(\dfrac{e}{2}\) (B) forgets that \(e^0 = 1\).
Key point: Change the limits with the substitution.

questions.sub_topic: Projection onto a vector of length 7
questions.question: The projection of \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\) on \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(5\)
Given: \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 2 - 9 + 42 = 35\), \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7\)
Formula: projection of \(\vec{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) \(= \dfrac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{35}{7} = 5\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{35}{\sqrt{59}}\) (A) divides by \(|\vec{a}|\), which gives the projection of \(\vec{b}\) on \(\vec{a}\). \(\dfrac{5}{7}\) (D) divides by \(|\vec{b}|^2\).
Key point: Divide by the length of the vector you project onto.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int e^{3x}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x} + C\)
Given: \(e^{ax}\) with \(a = 3\)
Formula: \(\int e^{ax}dx = \dfrac{1}{a}e^{ax} + C\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x} + C\)
Common mistake: (A) differentiates instead of integrating. (D) applies the power rule to an exponential.
Key point: Divide by the coefficient of \(x\) in the exponent.

questions.question: The minimum value of \(f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(-4\)
Given: \(f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5\)
Formula: \(f'(x) = 0\), \(f''(x) > 0\)
Step 1: \(f'(x) = 2x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 3\); \(f''(x) = 2 > 0\)
Step 2: \(f(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4\)
Common mistake: \(3\) (A) gives the point, not the value. \(5\) (B) is \(f(0)\).
Key point: The minimum value is \(f\) at the minimising point.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x + y}{x}\) is a homogeneous differential equation.
(B) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = x\) is a linear differential equation.
(C) \(\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^2 + \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\) has degree 2.
(D) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin(xy)\) is in variable separable form.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(\dfrac{x + y}{x} = 1 + \dfrac{y}{x}\) depends only on \(\dfrac{y}{x}\). (B) It has the form \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\). (C) The highest derivative is squared.
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(\sin(xy)\) cannot be written as \(f(x)g(y)\). Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Separable needs a product of a function of \(x\) and a function of \(y\).

questions.sub_topic: Unit vector in a given direction
questions.question: The unit vector in the direction of \(3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{1}{5}(3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j})\)
Given: \(\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j}\)
Formula: \(\hat{a} = \dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}\)
Step 1: \(|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\)
Step 2: \(\hat{a} = \dfrac{1}{5}(3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j})\)
Common mistake: (C) divides by \(|\vec{a}|^2\). (D) divides by \(3 + 4\).
Key point: Divide by the magnitude.

questions.sub_topic: Angle between lines with direction ratios 2, 2, 1 and 4, 1, 8
questions.question: The angle between two lines with direction ratios \(2, 2, 1\) and \(4, 1, 8\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\)
Given: \((a_1, b_1, c_1) = (2, 2, 1)\), \((a_2, b_2, c_2) = (4, 1, 8)\)
Formula: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}\)
Step 1: Numerator \(= 8 + 2 + 8 = 18\)
Step 2: Magnitudes \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(\sqrt{81} = 9\)
Step 3: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{18}{27} = \dfrac{2}{3}\), so \(\theta = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{9}\) (D) divides by \(9^2\) instead of \(3 \times 9\).
Key point: Divide by the product of both magnitudes.

questions.sub_topic: Related rates for a growing cube
questions.question: The volume of a cube increases at 9 cm³/s. How fast is its surface area increasing when the edge is 10 cm?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3.6\) cm²/s
Given: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 9\), \(a = 10\)
Formula: \(V = a^3\), \(S = 6a^2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 3a^2\dfrac{da}{dt} \Rightarrow 9 = 300\dfrac{da}{dt} \Rightarrow \dfrac{da}{dt} = 0.03\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt} = 12a\dfrac{da}{dt} = 120 \times 0.03 = 3.6\)
Common mistake: \(0.03\) (B) stops at the rate of the edge. \(1.8\) (C) uses \(\dfrac{dS}{da} = 6a\).
Key point: Link the two rates through \(\dfrac{da}{dt}\).

questions.sub_topic: First derivative for a parametric parabola
questions.question: If \(x = at^2\) and \(y = 2at\), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{1}{t}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2at\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2a\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2a}{2at} = \dfrac{1}{t}\)
Common mistake: \(t\) (B) divides the other way round, \(\dfrac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}\).
Key point: The \(y\)-derivative goes on top.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about square matrices of order 3:
(A) Interchanging two rows changes the sign of the determinant.
(B) \(|kA| = k|A|\).
(C) A determinant with two identical rows is zero.
(D) \(|AB| = |A||B|\).
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: for order 3, \(|kA| = k^3|A|\), since \(k\) comes out of each of the three rows.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are standard properties. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: \(|kA| = k^n|A|\) for a matrix of order \(n\).

questions.question: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{\sin x}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(e^{\sin x}\cos x\)
Given: outer \(e^u\), inner \(u = \sin x\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u} = e^{u}\dfrac{du}{dx}\)
Step 1: \(e^{\sin x}\cdot\cos x\)
Common mistake: (A) forgets the derivative of the inner function. (D) applies the power rule to an exponential.
Key point: \(e^u\) stays as it is; multiply by \(u'\).

questions.topic: Unit III: Applications of the Integrals
questions.sub_topic: Area cut off by x = 1 from y² = 4x
questions.question: The area of the region bounded by the parabola \(y^2 = 4x\) and the line \(x = 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) sq units
Given: \(y = \pm 2\sqrt{x}\); the region is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis
Formula: Area \(= 2\int_0^1 2\sqrt{x}\,dx\)
Step 1: \(\int_0^1 2\sqrt{x}\,dx = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\)
Step 2: Area \(= 2 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{4}{3}\) (A) takes only the half above the \(x\)-axis. \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) (D) integrates \(\sqrt{x}\) instead of \(2\sqrt{x}\).
Key point: Use the symmetry of \(y^2 = 4ax\) about the \(x\)-axis.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Function)
(A) \(\sin^{-1}x\)
(B) \(\cos^{-1}x\)
(C) \(\tan^{-1}x\)
(D) \(\cot^{-1}x\)

List-II (Principal value branch)
(I) \((0, \pi)\)
(II) \([0, \pi]\)
(III) \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)
(IV) \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: \(\sin^{-1}\) takes \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (at \(x = \pm 1\)), so its range is closed (IV); \(\cos^{-1}\) reaches 0 and \(\pi\) (II); \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so the range is open (III); \(\cot x\) is undefined at 0 and \(\pi\) (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the sine and tangent ranges. (B) swaps the cosine and cotangent ranges. (C) swaps the tangent and cotangent ranges.
Key point: The end points are included exactly when the original function is defined there.

questions.sub_topic: Properties of a relation on a three-element set
questions.question:
On \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\), let \(R = \{(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2)\}\). Consider the following statements:
(A) \(R\) is reflexive.
(B) \(R\) is symmetric.
(C) \(R\) is transitive.
(D) \(R\) is an equivalence relation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) and (C) only
Why: (A) All of \((1,1), (2,2), (3,3)\) are present. (C) The only chains are \((1,1),(1,2)\) and \((1,2),(2,2)\), and both give \((1,2) \in R\).
Why not the others: (B) is false: \((1,2) \in R\) but \((2,1) \notin R\). So (D) is false too. Option (C) leaves out (C); options (B) and (D) include a false statement.
Key point: An equivalence relation needs all three properties.

questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2y\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(y = Ce^{x^3}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = 3x^2dx\)
Formula: integrate both sides
Step 1: \(\log|y| = x^3 + c\)
Step 2: \(y = Ce^{x^3}\)
Common mistake: (C) puts \(3x^2\) in the exponent without integrating it. (D) adds the constant after taking the exponential.
Key point: \(e^{x^3 + c} = e^c \cdot e^{x^3}\), so the constant multiplies.

questions.sub_topic: Variance of a three-valued random variable
questions.question: \(X\) takes the values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. The variance of \(X\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(0.49\)
Given: values 1, 2, 3; probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3
Formula: \(\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2\)
Step 1: \(E(X) = 0.2 + 1.0 + 0.9 = 2.1\)
Step 2: \(E(X^2) = 0.2 + 2.0 + 2.7 = 4.9\)
Step 3: \(\text{Var}(X) = 4.9 - 4.41 = 0.49\)
Common mistake: \(2.1\) (A) is the mean. \(4.9\) (B) is \(E(X^2)\). \(0.7\) (D) is the standard deviation.
Key point: Subtract the square of the mean from the mean of the squares.

questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\), then \(AB\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\begin{bmatrix}4&6\\10&12\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: row of \(A\) times column of \(B\)
Formula: \((AB)_{ij} = \sum_k a_{ik}b_{kj}\)
Step 1: Row 1: \(2 + 2 = 4\); \(0 + 6 = 6\)
Step 2: Row 2: \(6 + 4 = 10\); \(0 + 12 = 12\)
Common mistake: (A) multiplies entry by entry. (B) is \(BA\). (C) is \(A + B\).
Key point: \(AB \ne BA\) in general.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.question: The solution set of \(|x - 3| < 2\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1 < x < 5\)
Given: \(|t| < a \iff -a < t < a\)
Formula: \(-2 < x - 3 < 2\)
Step 1: Add 3 throughout: \(1 < x < 5\)
Common mistake: (D) is the solution of \(|x - 3| > 2\). (C) drops the left half of the inequality.
Key point: "Less than" with a modulus gives a single interval.

questions.sub_topic: Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-test
questions.question: For a one-sample t-test on a sample of size 16, the degrees of freedom are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(15\)
Given: \(n = 16\)
Formula: d.f. \(= n - 1\)
Step 1: \(16 - 1 = 15\)
Common mistake: \(16\) (A) uses \(n\). \(14\) (B) uses \(n - 2\), which belongs to other tests.
Key point: One degree of freedom is used up in estimating the mean.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(23 \bmod 5\)
(B) \(7^2 \bmod 4\)
(C) \(100 \bmod 7\)
(D) \((15 \times 4) \bmod 7\)

List-II
(I) \(2\)
(II) \(4\)
(III) \(1\)
(IV) \(3\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Given: \(a \bmod n\) is the remainder when \(a\) is divided by \(n\)
Step 1: \(23 = 4 \times 5 + 3\) → 3 (IV)
Step 2: \(49 = 12 \times 4 + 1\) → 1 (III)
Step 3: \(100 = 14 \times 7 + 2\) → 2 (I)
Step 4: \(60 = 8 \times 7 + 4\) → 4 (II)
Common mistake: (B) swaps the first two. (C) swaps \(7^2\) and 100. (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Reduce the product first, or reduce each factor and multiply again.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int\left(x^2 + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{x^3}{3} + \log|x| + C\)
Given: integrate term by term
Formula: \(\int x^n dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\) (\(n \ne -1\)), \(\int \dfrac{dx}{x} = \log|x|\)
Step 1: \(\int x^2dx = \dfrac{x^3}{3}\); \(\int \dfrac{dx}{x} = \log|x|\)
Common mistake: (A) differentiates. (B) applies the power rule to \(x^{-1}\), which is not allowed.
Key point: \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) is the one power that integrates to a logarithm.

questions.sub_topic: Binomial probability of exactly one success
questions.question: For a binomial distribution with \(n = 5\) and \(p = \dfrac{1}{3}\), \(P(X = 1)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{80}{243}\)
Given: \(n = 5\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{3}\), \(q = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
Formula: \(P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r}p^rq^{n-r}\)
Step 1: \(\binom{5}{1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^4 = 5 \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{16}{81}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{80}{243}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{16}{243}\) (A) forgets \(\binom{5}{1} = 5\). \(\dfrac{32}{243}\) (C) is \(P(X = 0) = q^5\).
Key point: Count the arrangements with \(\binom{n}{r}\).

questions.sub_topic: Expected score on a fair die
questions.question: The expected value of the number shown on a fair six-sided die is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3.5\)
Given: each face has probability \(\dfrac{1}{6}\)
Formula: \(E(X) = \sum xP(X = x)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{6} = \dfrac{21}{6} = 3.5\)
Common mistake: \(21\) (C) forgets to multiply by \(\dfrac{1}{6}\). \(3\) (B) rounds down to a face value.
Key point: The expected value need not be a possible outcome.

questions.question: The three-yearly moving averages of the values 10, 14, 12, 16, 20 are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 12, 14, 16
Given: values 10, 14, 12, 16, 20
Formula: average each run of three consecutive values
Step 1: \(\dfrac{10 + 14 + 12}{3} = 12\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{14 + 12 + 16}{3} = 14\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{12 + 16 + 20}{3} = 16\)
Common mistake: (D) gives the moving totals without dividing by 3. (C) gives four-yearly averages.
Key point: Five values give three three-yearly averages.

questions.question: The total cost of producing \(x\) units is \(C(x) = x^2 + 100\). The minimum average cost is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(20\)
Given: \(AC(x) = \dfrac{C(x)}{x} = x + \dfrac{100}{x}\)
Formula: \(AC'(x) = 0\), \(AC''(x) > 0\)
Step 1: \(AC'(x) = 1 - \dfrac{100}{x^2} = 0 \Rightarrow x = 10\)
Step 2: \(AC''(x) = \dfrac{200}{x^3} > 0\), so this is a minimum
Step 3: \(AC(10) = 10 + 10 = 20\)
Common mistake: \(10\) (A) is the output, not the average cost. \(200\) (C) is the total cost at \(x = 10\).
Key point: Minimise the average cost, not the total cost.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In a diet problem, the objective is usually to minimise cost.
(B) Non-negativity restrictions are used because the quantities cannot be negative.
(C) In a transportation problem, the objective is usually to minimise the total transport cost.
(D) The constraints of a linear programming problem may contain terms such as \(x^2\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) describe standard LPP formulations correctly.
Why not the others: (D) is false: every constraint of an LPP must be linear. Options (B) and (C) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: "Linear" applies to the objective function and to every constraint.

questions.sub_topic: Shifting the origin of a trend equation
questions.question: A trend equation is \(y = 120 + 8x\), with origin 2022 and \(x\) in years. With the origin shifted to 2024, the equation becomes:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(y = 136 + 8x\)
Given: 2024 is 2 years after 2022
Formula: replace \(x\) by \(x + 2\)
Step 1: \(y = 120 + 8(x + 2) = 136 + 8x\)
Common mistake: (A) shifts the wrong way (\(x - 2\)). (C) shifts by one year only. (D) changes the slope.
Key point: Shifting the origin changes the intercept, not the slope.

questions.sub_topic: Maximum profit from chairs and tables
questions.question: A workshop makes chairs (profit ₹30 each) and tables (profit ₹50 each). A chair takes 1 hour and a table 2 hours, and 20 hours are available. At most 10 chairs can be sold. The maximum profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹550
Given: maximise \(Z = 30x + 50y\) subject to \(x + 2y \le 20\), \(x \le 10\), \(x, y \ge 0\)
Formula: evaluate \(Z\) at the corner points
Step 1: Corners: \((0, 0)\), \((10, 0)\), \((10, 5)\), \((0, 10)\)
Step 2: \(Z = 0, 300, 550, 500\)
Step 3: Maximum ₹550 at 10 chairs and 5 tables
Common mistake: ₹500 (A) makes only tables. ₹600 (D) makes 20 chairs, ignoring \(x \le 10\).
Key point: Include every limit (here the sales limit) as a constraint.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Present value of a perpetuity of ₹500 a year at 5%
(B) Annual straight-line depreciation: cost ₹50,000, scrap ₹10,000, life 8 years
(C) CAGR when ₹1,000 grows to ₹1,210 in 2 years
(D) Amount of ₹1,000 after 2 years at 10% compounded annually

List-II
(I) \(10\%\)
(II) ₹10,000
(III) ₹1,210
(IV) ₹5,000
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Step 1: Perpetuity \(= \dfrac{500}{0.05} = ₹10{,}000\) (II)
Step 2: Depreciation \(= \dfrac{50{,}000 - 10{,}000}{8} = ₹5{,}000\) (IV)
Step 3: CAGR \(= \left(\dfrac{1210}{1000}\right)^{1/2} - 1 = 1.1 - 1 = 10\%\) (I)
Step 4: Amount \(= 1000(1.1)^2 = ₹1{,}210\) (III)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the perpetuity and the depreciation. (C) swaps the CAGR and the amount. (D) swaps the depreciation and the CAGR.
Key point: The same numbers can answer different questions; read what each item asks.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.question: Rice costing ₹50 per kg is mixed with rice costing ₹65 per kg in the ratio \(2 : 3\). The price of the mixture per kg is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹59
Given: 2 kg at ₹50 and 3 kg at ₹65
Formula: mean price \(= \dfrac{\text{total cost}}{\text{total quantity}}\)
Step 1: Total cost \(= 100 + 195 = ₹295\)
Step 2: Mean price \(= \dfrac{295}{5} = ₹59\)
Common mistake: ₹57.50 (B) takes the simple average of the two prices. ₹56 (C) attaches the ratio to the wrong prices.
Key point: Weight each price by its quantity.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a time series:
(A) Cyclical variations have a period of more than one year.
(B) Irregular variations can be predicted in advance.
(C) Seasonal variations repeat within a year.
(D) The trend shows the long-term movement of the series.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: irregular variations come from unforeseen events such as floods or strikes, so they cannot be predicted.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) describe the components correctly. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Trend, seasonal and cyclical parts have patterns; the irregular part does not.

questions.question: For a Poisson distribution with mean 2, \(P(X = 0)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(e^{-2}\)
Given: \(\lambda = 2\)
Formula: \(P(X = r) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}\)
Step 1: \(P(X = 0) = \dfrac{e^{-2}\cdot 2^0}{0!} = e^{-2}\)
Common mistake: \(2e^{-2}\) (A) is \(P(X = 1)\). \(1 - e^{-2}\) (D) is \(P(X \ge 1)\).
Key point: \(\lambda^0 = 1\) and \(0! = 1\).

questions.sub_topic: Equal instalment for a two-year loan
questions.question: A loan of ₹21,000 is repaid in 2 equal annual instalments at 10% per annum compounded annually. Each instalment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹12,100
Given: \(P = 21{,}000\), \(i = 0.1\), \(n = 2\)
Formula: EMI \(= \dfrac{Pi(1 + i)^n}{(1 + i)^n - 1}\)
Step 1: \((1.1)^2 = 1.21\)
Step 2: EMI \(= \dfrac{21{,}000 \times 0.1 \times 1.21}{0.21} = \dfrac{2541}{0.21} = 12{,}100\)
Step 3: Check: after one year \(23{,}100 - 12{,}100 = 11{,}000\); after two years \(12{,}100 - 12{,}100 = 0\) ✓
Common mistake: ₹10,500 (A) ignores interest. ₹12,705 (D) compounds the whole loan for 2 years and then halves it.
Key point: Each instalment reduces the balance on which interest is charged.

questions.question: A sample gives the values 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. To test \(H_0: \mu = 6\), the t-statistic (using \(s\) with divisor \(n - 1\)) is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1.41\)
Given: \(n = 5\), \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{40}{5} = 8\)
Formula: \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\), \(t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}\)
Step 1: Deviations \(-4, -2, 0, 2, 4\); squares add to \(40\)
Step 2: \(s^2 = \dfrac{40}{4} = 10\), \(s = \sqrt{10}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{2}\)
Step 4: \(t = \dfrac{8 - 6}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\)
Common mistake: \(1.58\) (D) uses divisor \(n\) (\(s^2 = 8\)). \(0.63\) (C) divides by \(s\) instead of \(s/\sqrt{n}\). \(2\) (B) is just \(\bar{x} - \mu\).
Key point: Use \(n - 1\) for \(s\) and divide by the standard error.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Race decided by metres and seconds
questions.question: In a 200 m race, A beats B by 20 m or by 4 seconds. The time A takes to run the race is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(36\) s
Given: B covers the last 20 m in 4 s
Formula: speed = distance ÷ time
Step 1: B's speed \(= \dfrac{20}{4} = 5\) m/s
Step 2: B's time for 200 m \(= \dfrac{200}{5} = 40\) s
Step 3: A finishes 4 s earlier: \(40 - 4 = 36\) s
Common mistake: \(40\) s (A) is B's time. \(44\) s (D) adds the 4 s instead of subtracting.
Key point: "20 m or 4 s" means B needs 4 s for those 20 m.

questions.question: A population has standard deviation 12. The standard error of the mean of a random sample of size 36 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2\)
Given: \(\sigma = 12\), \(n = 36\)
Formula: SE \(= \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{36}} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) (A) divides by \(n\) instead of \(\sqrt{n}\). \(6\) (C) is \(\sqrt{n}\) itself.
Key point: The standard error shrinks as \(\sqrt{n}\) grows.

questions.sub_topic: A 2 × 2 system by the inverse matrix
questions.question: Using \(X = A^{-1}B\), the solution of \(2x + y = 5\) and \(x - y = 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x = 2, y = 1\)
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}5\\1\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 1: \(|A| = -2 - 1 = -3\); \(A^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(X = -\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-5 - 1\\-5 + 2\end{bmatrix} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-6\\-3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\)
Common mistake: (B) swaps \(x\) and \(y\). (D) loses a sign in the second row.
Key point: Substitute back to check: \(4 + 1 = 5\) ✓, \(2 - 1 = 1\) ✓.

questions.sub_topic: Annual deposit for a sinking fund
questions.question: How much must be deposited at the end of each year at 10% compounded annually to accumulate ₹33,100 in 3 years?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹10,000
Given: \(A = 33{,}100\), \(i = 0.1\), \(n = 3\)
Formula: \(A = R\left[\dfrac{(1 + i)^n - 1}{i}\right]\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{(1.1)^3 - 1}{0.1} = \dfrac{0.331}{0.1} = 3.31\)
Step 2: \(R = \dfrac{33{,}100}{3.31} = 10{,}000\)
Common mistake: ₹11,033 (A) divides the target by 3 and ignores interest.
Key point: Interest earned by earlier deposits lowers the deposit needed.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_1^2(4x^3 - 6x)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(6\)
Given: antiderivative \(F(x) = x^4 - 3x^2\)
Formula: \(\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)\)
Step 1: \(F(2) = 16 - 12 = 4\)
Step 2: \(F(1) = 1 - 3 = -2\)
Step 3: \(F(2) - F(1) = 4 - (-2) = 6\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (B) ignores the lower limit. \(2\) (A) subtracts \(+2\) instead of \(-2\).
Key point: A negative value at the lower limit increases the result.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Speed in still water from upstream and downstream
questions.question: A boat's upstream speed is 8 km/h and its downstream speed is 12 km/h. Its speed in still water is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(10\) km/h
Given: \(u - v = 8\), \(u + v = 12\)
Formula: \(u = \dfrac{\text{downstream} + \text{upstream}}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{12 + 8}{2} = 10\) km/h
Common mistake: \(2\) km/h (A) is the speed of the stream. \(20\) km/h (B) forgets to halve the sum.
Key point: Half the sum gives the boat's speed; half the difference gives the stream's.

questions.sub_topic: Consumer surplus with a quadratic demand
questions.question: The demand function is \(p = 50 - x^2\). The consumer surplus when the quantity demanded is 5 units is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹\(\dfrac{250}{3}\)
Given: \(x_0 = 5\), \(p_0 = 50 - 25 = 25\)
Formula: CS \(= \int_0^{x_0}D(x)\,dx - p_0x_0\)
Step 1: \(\int_0^5(50 - x^2)dx = 250 - \dfrac{125}{3} = \dfrac{625}{3}\)
Step 2: \(p_0x_0 = 25 \times 5 = 125\)
Step 3: CS \(= \dfrac{625}{3} - 125 = \dfrac{250}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{625}{3}\) (B) is the area under the demand curve, without subtracting the expenditure. \(125\) (C) is the expenditure \(p_0x_0\).
Key point: Consumer surplus is the area between the demand curve and the price line.

questions.question: \(A\) is a square matrix of order 3 with \(|A| = 5\). Then \(|3\,\text{adj}\,A|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(675\)
Given: \(n = 3\), \(|A| = 5\)
Formula: \(|\text{adj}\,A| = |A|^{n-1}\), \(|kB| = k^n|B|\)
Step 1: \(|\text{adj}\,A| = 5^2 = 25\)
Step 2: \(|3\,\text{adj}\,A| = 3^3 \times 25 = 675\)
Common mistake: \(75\) (A) takes \(k\) instead of \(k^3\). \(135\) (D) uses \(|\text{adj}\,A| = |A|\).
Key point: Two rules apply here: one for the scalar, one for the adjoint.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: A filling pipe and an emptying pipe
questions.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours and pipe B empties it in 18 hours. If both are opened together on an empty tank, it fills in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(36\) hours
Given: A's rate \(= +\dfrac{1}{12}\), B's rate \(= -\dfrac{1}{18}\)
Formula: net rate = filling rate − emptying rate
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{36} = \dfrac{1}{36}\)
Step 2: Time \(= 36\) hours
Common mistake: \(7.2\) hours (B) adds the two rates. \(6\) hours (A) subtracts the times.
Key point: An emptying pipe's rate is negative.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a normal distribution:
(A) Its mean, median and mode are equal.
(B) Its curve is symmetric about the mean.
(C) The total area under its curve is 1.
(D) About 50% of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are basic properties of the normal curve.
Why not the others: (D) is false: about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation; 50% lie on each side of the mean. Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: 68–95–99.7 for one, two and three standard deviations.

questions.question: The function \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\) is strictly increasing on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)\)
Given: \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)\)
Formula: increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\)
Step 1: \(f'(x) > 0\) when \(x < -1\) or \(x > 1\)
Common mistake: (B) is where \(f\) is decreasing. (C) only checks where \(f'\) is positive for large \(x\).
Key point: Mark the critical points on a number line and test the sign on each part.

questions.question:
For the revenue function \(R(x) = 20x - x^2\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Marginal revenue function
(B) Marginal revenue at \(x = 3\)
(C) Output at which marginal revenue is zero
(D) Maximum revenue

List-II
(I) \(100\)
(II) \(20 - 2x\)
(III) \(14\)
(IV) \(10\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Given: \(R(x) = 20x - x^2\)
Step 1: MR \(= R'(x) = 20 - 2x\) (II)
Step 2: MR at \(x = 3\): \(20 - 6 = 14\) (III)
Step 3: \(20 - 2x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 10\) (IV)
Step 4: \(R(10) = 200 - 100 = 100\) (I)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the function and its value. (B) swaps MR at 3 and the output. (D) swaps the output and the maximum revenue.
Key point: Revenue is greatest where marginal revenue is zero.

questions.question: If \(y = e^{2x}\), then \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(4e^{2x}\)
Given: \(y = e^{2x}\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{ax} = ae^{ax}\)
Step 1: \(y' = 2e^{2x}\)
Step 2: \(y'' = 4e^{2x}\)
Common mistake: \(2e^{2x}\) (A) is the first derivative only.
Key point: Each differentiation brings out another factor of 2.

questions.question: An investment earns a nominal return of 9% per annum while inflation is 4% per annum. The real rate of return is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(5\%\)
Given: nominal rate 9%, inflation 4%
Formula: real rate \(\approx\) nominal rate − inflation rate
Step 1: \(9\% - 4\% = 5\%\)
Common mistake: \(13\%\) (B) adds inflation instead of subtracting it. \(2.25\%\) (C) divides the two rates.
Key point: The exact value \(\dfrac{1.09}{1.04} - 1 \approx 4.8\%\) is close to the approximation.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A symmetric matrix satisfies \(A^T = A\).
(B) Every diagonal matrix is a scalar matrix.
(C) The identity matrix is a diagonal matrix.
(D) Every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: \(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\) is diagonal but not scalar, because its diagonal entries differ.
Why not the others: (A) is the definition. (C) \(I\) has zeros off the diagonal. (D) \(a_{ii} = -a_{ii}\) forces \(a_{ii} = 0\). Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Every scalar matrix is diagonal, but not the other way round.
